messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 75
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Auditor
  trauma_type: Civilian in war zone
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Sweat/Body): Sweat or body odour, Feeling Happy: Feeling happy or relaxed, Workplace: Workplace
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Prevention: ruminate about how event could have been prevented, Rumination: Meaning: go over and over why the event happened to me, Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction
  Threat: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
  Memory: Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
  Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me, Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore, Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Eileen, a 75-year-old Oceania-born woman who had spent much of her adult life working as an auditor, described how the war had entered her life in the ordinary, humiliating spaces where she had once tried to keep order. During a bombing in the city where she was living as a civilian, she became separated from her husband in the confusion and spent hours moving through damaged streets and crowded shelters, trying to account for people and papers while the smell of sweat, unwashed bodies, dust, and fear clung to the air. She said that when she thinks of it now, the memory comes back “like photographs,” fixed and stark, and yet she cannot find words for what happened in a way that feels adequate; she knows it happened, but the experience sits in her mind as vivid scenes and sensations rather than a story she can tell. The smell of sweat or body odour, even now in a busy room, can throw her back into those images, and moments of feeling happy or relaxed can do the same, because she becomes abruptly aware of how vulnerable she was when she had briefly let herself feel safe. Those reminders have fed the thought that others can see what happened to her just by looking at her, as if the terror were written on her face, and she has come to believe that her life is not worth living anymore and that she will never be able to feel normal emotions again.

Since then, Eileen has become preoccupied with what the event meant and how it might have been avoided. She goes over and over, in a painstaking and self-reproaching way, why it happened to her and how she might have prevented it, replaying every decision from the day of the attack, every route she took, every delay, and every choice she made while trying to preserve a sense of control. That rumination keeps the scene alive in a vividly visual form: the more she searches for a reason, the more she sees those same photographic fragments, and the more she tries to put the experience into words, the more the images take over. The act of thinking it through has only deepened her sense that something terrible was exposed in her, something others can detect immediately, and it has strengthened her belief that she is changed in a permanent, visible way. At night she often lies awake reviewing it all, and the memory of the event is intensified rather than settled by this effort to explain it.

Her sense of danger has become organized around those appraisals. Eileen sits with her back against a wall whenever she can, scanning the room so that no one can come up behind her, and she frequently looks over her shoulder as though someone might be following her. In the workplace, where she still tries to do bookkeeping and audit-related tasks in a small office, she chooses seats that give her a clear view of the door and avoids being trapped in the middle of a meeting room; the smell of sweat from a crowded corridor or the sudden ease of a calm afternoon can be enough to make her tense, alert, and ready to bolt. What frightens her most is that if she relaxes, she will be caught off guard again, and that fear has begun to shape her behavior in risky, almost self-defeating ways, as though she were testing whether danger will find her anyway. Even while she is trying to keep herself safe, her mind stays on guard, and every glance behind her or shift of a chair back toward the wall seems to confirm how unsafe she feels.

These strategies, however, have not settled her. The rehearsing of conversations before any interaction has made even simple exchanges feel loaded and unnatural, and she often leaves the encounter more aware of herself than of the other person, more convinced that others can tell something happened to her. Her repeated mental reviews of how it could have been prevented and why it happened to her have not brought relief; they have deepened her hopelessness and made her feel that normal emotions are no longer available to her. Each time the memory returns, she becomes more vigilant, and that vigilance, in turn, pulls the images back into focus, so that the photographs in her mind and the bodily feeling of being watched keep reappearing together. The cycle has narrowed her world and made her husband worry, because she is less able to settle into ordinary conversation, more easily startled by the atmosphere of a room, and increasingly withdrawn from the very moments of feeling safe that once gave her some respite.

By the time she sought help, Eileen said she was exhausted by the constant effort of bracing herself, replaying the event, and trying to keep her composure in public. She wanted relief from the sense that her face betrays what happened to her and from the conviction that she will never feel normal again, but she was also afraid that if she stopped checking, stopped replaying, or stopped positioning herself defensively, the memory would flood back with the force of the war zone all over again.
